network.overall_strategy: Construct the threonine carbon skeleton by cyanide homologation of acetaldehyde to lactaldehyde, followed by Strecker chemistry or hydantoin-mediated amino-acid formation. The ten pathways are distinct operational graph paths, not ten independently validated prebiotic syntheses: they combine two photoredox donor systems, imine-first versus cyanohydrin-storage entry, and alternative hydrolysis regimes. Cyanohydrin-storage pathways return to the same imine manifold and do not represent a new carbon–nitrogen bond-forming mechanism. Selective lactonitrile photoreduction and sufficiently rapid hydantoin deprotection are important conditional bottlenecks; no complete end-to-end prebiotic synthesis is claimed to have been demonstrated. All processes are anoxic, and no enzymes or molecular oxygen are assumed. The designated target is L-threonine, but achiral chemistry also produces D-threonine and allo-threonines; no enantiomeric enrichment or threo-selective isolation is asserted. Unspecified stereochemistry in precursor nodes denotes unresolved stereochemical pools. Product lists enumerate possible stereoisomers without specifying their proportions. Neutral parent formulas are used where practical, with aqueous protonation and spectator counterions implicit. Because the schema lacks a coproduct role, non-target terminal products are labeled intermediate. For species formed in multiple settings, environment_formed records the principal setting, while reaction nodes identify additional formation environments.

reactions.name: Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Anoxic, mildly alkaline solution, approximately pH 8-9; cyanide is supplied by HCN dissociation. Volatile feedstocks require replenishment or retention in covered pores.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the acetaldehyde carbonyl, followed by proton transfer to form racemic lactonitrile. The addition is reversible.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanohydrin formation is established carbonyl chemistry and provides the correct carbon connectivity for a one-carbon homologation to lactaldehyde. No mineral catalyst is required. Dilution, HCN loss, acetaldehyde volatility, and competing nitrile hydrolysis limit accumulation; equilibrium conversion is not assumed to be quantitative.

reactions.name: Conditional sulfide-driven photoreductive homologation of lactonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic UV irradiation, approximately 200-280 nm; mildly alkaline conditions with available sulfide/hydrosulfide. Irradiation must be limited to reduce aldehyde overreaction.

reactions.mechanism: Photochemical electron transfer reduces the nitrile functionality to an imine-level intermediate, whose hydrolysis releases lactaldehyde and ammonia. Sulfide supplies reducing equivalents; elemental sulfur is the idealized oxidized sulfur endpoint represented here.
reactions.reasoning: UV-driven cyanohydrin reductive homologation is supported as a reaction class by Ritson and Sutherland (2013) and Patel et al. (2015). Recoverable lactaldehyde production from this particular substrate under the stated conditions is treated as a conditional extrapolation, not an established end-to-end threonine synthesis. Copper-cyanide complexes are included for their photoredox function, not as generic mineral catalysts. Overreduction, sulfur adduct formation, and mixed sulfur products are important uncertainties; S8 represents one balanced limiting product branch.

reactions.name: Conditional sulfite-ferrocyanide photoreductive homologation of lactonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic UV irradiation, approximately 200-280 nm; sulfite-rich, approximately pH 7-9 solution. Sulfite regenerates the reduced photoredox system.

reactions.mechanism: Photogenerated reducing equivalents convert the nitrile to an imine-level intermediate, followed by hydrolysis to lactaldehyde and ammonia. Sulfite oxidation to sulfate closes the represented net electron balance without molecular oxygen.
reactions.reasoning: Sulfite-ferrocyanide photochemical reductive homologation is supported at the reaction-class level by Xu et al. (2018). Applying it selectively to lactonitrile is a substrate-specific hypothesis requiring experimental verification. Ferrocyanide is chemically justified as a light-responsive Fe(II) complex; free iron minerals are not assumed to perform the same function. Sulfate is one modeled oxidation endpoint, and competing sulfur-radical products and aldehyde destruction can lower yield.

reactions.name: Lactaldehyde imine formation

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8-9, concentrated ammoniacal solution; subsequent cyanide trapping is needed because imine formation is reversible in water.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde, forming a carbinolamine that loses water to give the imine/iminium pool.
reactions.reasoning: This is the conventional carbonyl-ammonia entry to Strecker chemistry (Strecker, 1850). It does not require an enzyme or an assumed mineral catalyst. Lactaldehyde hydration, oligomerization, and the low equilibrium abundance of free imine are limitations; downstream cyanide trapping, rather than complete isolation of the imine, supplies the productive sink.

reactions.name: Cyanide capture of lactaldehyde imine

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8-9 with both cyanide and imine/iminium available; avoid prolonged irradiation after the aminonitrile has accumulated.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the imine/iminium carbon, followed by proton transfer to produce 2-amino-3-hydroxybutanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The bond construction follows established Strecker chemistry (Strecker, 1850). The original aldehyde carbon becomes the amino-bearing alpha carbon, while cyanide becomes the eventual carboxyl carbon. This mapping gives threonine-family connectivity rather than homoserine. Racemic lactaldehyde and nonchiral conditions produce unresolved diastereomers and enantiomers; selective formation of L-threonine is not supported.

reactions.name: Lactaldehyde capture as a cyanohydrin reservoir

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8-9; cyanide-rich conditions before substantial ammonia addition. The cyanohydrin remains in equilibrium with lactaldehyde.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to lactaldehyde produces 2,3-dihydroxybutanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Ordinary cyanohydrin chemistry supports this alternative speciation state. It is included as a potentially useful aldehyde reservoir when cyanide arrives before ammonia, not as an independently established threonine synthesis. Any protective benefit against aldehyde side reactions is conditional: reservoir stability, nitrile hydrolysis, and recovery on ammoniation require measurement.

reactions.name: Ammonia-driven transfer from cyanohydrin reservoir to imine

conditions.other: Concentrated ammoniacal solution, approximately pH 8-9; coupled to subsequent imine capture in rxn_005.

reactions.mechanism: This net pool-conversion step combines cyanohydrin dissociation with ammonia capture of the released aldehyde and dehydration to the imine. HCN is released and can be reused during aminonitrile formation.
reactions.reasoning: The chemically justified interpretation is reversible carbonyl release followed by the same imine chemistry used in the imine-first route. Direct displacement of an unactivated hydroxyl group by ammonia is not assumed. This is an operational feed-order alternative, not a distinct elementary Strecker mechanism; its usefulness depends on cyanohydrin release being faster than irreversible side reactions.

reactions.name: Aminonitrile hydration to threoninamide-family intermediates
agents: Hydronium in the acidic branch or hydroxide in the alkaline branch

conditions.catalyst: Acid or base promotion, used as alternatives
conditions.other: Acidic processing at approximately pH 0-2 or alkaline processing at approximately pH 10-12. The selected regime continues into rxn_009 or rxn_010, respectively; an acid-to-base switch is not required.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-promoted water addition or base-promoted hydroxide addition to the nitrile, followed by proton transfers and tautomerization, gives the corresponding amide.
reactions.reasoning: Sequential nitrile-to-amide-to-carboxyl hydrolysis is established chemistry underlying Strecker amino-acid preparation. The amide is a mechanistic intermediate and need not be isolated. Efficient hydrolysis at the milder end of these geochemical conditions is uncertain; prolonged exposure may instead cause decomposition or stereochemical scrambling. Near-neutral water is not assumed to hydrolyze the nitrile rapidly.

reactions.name: Acidic threoninamide hydrolysis
agents: Hydronium supplied by an acidic volcanic fluid

conditions.other: Approximately pH 0-2, with prolonged residence in an acidic hot pool. Actual amino-acid and ammonia products are predominantly protonated.

reactions.mechanism: Protonation activates the amide carbonyl for water addition; collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate releases the amino-acid carboxyl group and ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: Acidic amide hydrolysis is chemically established and needs no oxygen or enzyme. Strongly acidic volcanic waters offer a possible setting, although dilution and residence time may make conversion inefficient. Hydrolysis does not establish the desired stereochemistry: the four listed amino acids represent possible members of the inherited product pool, not a specified equimolar mixture.

reactions.name: Alkaline threoninamide hydrolysis

conditions.other: Approximately pH 10-12 in a concentrated alkaline pool. Products are principally carboxylates; neutral formulas represent the corresponding parent species.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide addition to the amide carbonyl produces a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to the amino-acid carboxylate and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Base-promoted amide hydrolysis is a genuine alternative to acidic processing and avoids requiring an acidic pool. Alkalinity is supplied by the environment rather than an unspecified mineral catalyst. In explicit ionic bookkeeping, hydroxide is consumed in forming carboxylate; the displayed neutral-parent equation is the net hydrolysis convention. Slow conversion, racemization, and degradation remain competing processes.

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs capture of the aminonitrile as a hydantoin

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with continued dissolved inorganic carbon supply
conditions.other: Concentrated ammoniacal carbonate/bicarbonate solution, approximately pH 8-9. CO2 represents the incorporated dissolved inorganic carbon.

reactions.mechanism: The aminonitrile undergoes N-carboxylation, intramolecular cyclization, and rearrangement through carbamate-derived intermediates to the hydantoin. These transformations are lumped into one net reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile-to-hydantoin conversion is part of established Bucherer-Bergs chemistry (Bucherer and Lieb, 1934). The incorporated carbon dioxide supplies the additional hydantoin carbonyl, so no hidden urea or activated carbamoyl reagent is assumed. Application to this hydroxy-substituted substrate in dilute natural waters is conditional. Hydantoin formation may stabilize the precursor, but it creates a harder downstream hydrolysis problem.

reactions.name: Hydantoin ring opening to N-carbamoyl amino acids
agents: Hydroxide supplied by alkaline hydrothermal fluid

conditions.other: Approximately pH 10-11 in a cooler alkaline hydrothermal zone, not a black-smoker endmember. Heating is introduced to address the hydrolysis barrier.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic attack at the hydantoin carbonyl adjacent to the substituted carbon opens the ring, producing an N-carbamoyl amino-acid carboxylate.
reactions.reasoning: Hydantoin ring opening to N-carbamoyl amino acids is established chemical behavior, but preparative nonenzymatic hydrolysis often uses stronger treatment than a natural alkaline fluid provides. Thus useful conversion in the stated geochemical window is conditional. The hydrothermal setting is included specifically for this kinetic requirement, not to force cross-environment connectivity. Ring-opening regioselectivity, reverse cyclization, and substrate survival are unresolved constraints.

reactions.name: Nonenzymatic N-carbamoyl removal
agents: Hydroxide supplied by alkaline hydrothermal fluid

conditions.other: Approximately pH 10-11; sufficiently long residence is required, followed by cooling if amino acids survive. CO2 denotes inorganic carbon released principally as bicarbonate/carbonate.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the carbamoyl substituent releases the amino acid and carbamic-acid-derived products, represented overall as ammonia and carbon dioxide.
reactions.reasoning: This is the least secure step of the hydantoin pathways. Nonenzymatic hydantoin-to-amino-acid preparations establish the overall chemistry, but they do not demonstrate efficient deprotection of this substrate within the specified natural-fluid window. N-carbamoyl cleavage may be slower than amino-acid decomposition or racemization, so this node is a speculative geochemical implementation rather than a demonstrated productive vent reaction. No carbamoylase enzyme or spontaneous rapid deprotection is assumed.

pathways.name: Sulfide photoredox, imine-first, acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde is homologated using the sulfide photoredox branch. Lactaldehyde enters the imine-first Strecker manifold, and the aminonitrile is hydrolyzed through the amide under acidic conditions. Conditional on selective lactonitrile reduction.

pathways.name: Sulfide photoredox, imine-first, alkaline hydrolysis
pathways.description: The same sulfide-supported carbon-skeleton assembly is followed by alkaline nitrile and amide hydrolysis. This is a processing alternative to P1, not an independent carbon-skeleton mechanism.

pathways.name: Sulfite photoredox, imine-first, acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: Sulfite and ferrocyanide replace the sulfide/copper photoredox system. The resulting lactaldehyde undergoes imine formation, cyanide capture, and acidic hydrolysis. Substrate-specific photoreduction selectivity remains conditional.

pathways.name: Sulfite photoredox, imine-first, alkaline hydrolysis
pathways.description: Sulfite-supported aldehyde homologation is coupled to imine-first Strecker chemistry and alkaline hydrolysis. This route uses a different electron-donor system from P2 and a different hydrolysis regime from P3.

pathways.name: Sulfide photoredox, cyanohydrin reservoir, acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: Lactaldehyde generated by sulfide photoredox chemistry is temporarily captured as its cyanohydrin before ammoniation. Reservoir release enters the shared imine manifold, followed by acidic hydrolysis. The reservoir is a conditional staging option, not a new Strecker mechanism.

pathways.name: Sulfide photoredox, cyanohydrin reservoir, alkaline hydrolysis
pathways.description: The sulfide-derived lactaldehyde cyanohydrin serves as a reversible feedstock reservoir. Ammonia-driven transfer to the imine is followed by cyanide capture and alkaline hydrolysis without requiring an acid-to-base processing switch.

pathways.name: Sulfite photoredox, cyanohydrin reservoir, acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: Sulfite-ferrocyanide photochemistry supplies lactaldehyde, which is captured before ammonia becomes abundant. Subsequent reservoir release, imine trapping, and acidic hydrolysis provide a graph-distinct operational route sharing the same central Strecker chemistry.

pathways.name: Sulfite photoredox, cyanohydrin reservoir, alkaline hydrolysis
pathways.description: This combines the sulfite electron donor, cyanohydrin-first feed order, and alkaline hydrolysis. Productive operation requires reversible reservoir release and hydrolysis to outcompete decomposition.

pathways.name: Sulfide photoredox followed by hydantoin capture and deprotection
pathways.description: Sulfide-derived lactaldehyde enters the imine-first aminonitrile route, followed by carbon dioxide incorporation into a hydantoin. Hydrothermal ring opening and carbamoyl removal replace direct nitrile hydrolysis. This pathway is especially conditional because thermal deprotection may lose the amino acid faster than it releases it.

pathways.name: Sulfite photoredox followed by hydantoin capture and deprotection
pathways.description: Sulfite-ferrocyanide photochemistry supplies the aldehyde precursor, while hydantoin formation provides the alternative downstream processing route. Both selective aldehyde production and nonenzymatic carbamoyl removal require validation under the stated conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The carbon skeleton and Strecker sequence are coherent, and all reactions conserve atoms and charge under the supplied check. Selective sulfide-driven lactonitrile reduction remains the principal unresolved step. Aminonitrile hydration and acidic amide hydrolysis are plausible, but their operating conditions and product survival are unspecified. L-threonine could occur within the unresolved stereoisomer mixture.
suggestions: Measure lactaldehyde yield and competing products from lactonitrile under specified anoxic irradiation, sulfide speciation, and light-absorber conditions.
Specify concentrations, pH, temperature, and residence times for imine trapping and subsequent acidic hydrolysis, including volatile-reactant retention.
Quantify amino-acid recovery and distinguish threonine from allothreonine and their enantiomers.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a coherent Strecker route with an alkaline hydrolysis finish. The supplied conservation check identifies no violations. Lactonitrile photoreduction is conditional, while productive nitrile and amide hydrolysis requires more than an unspecified surface-water environment. No evidence supplied establishes an advantage over the acidic finish.
suggestions: Demonstrate substrate-specific lactonitrile photoreduction and determine whether lactaldehyde survives continued irradiation.
Specify the alkalinity source, temperature, reaction duration, and transition from Strecker conditions to hydrolysis conditions.
Measure amino-acid yield and decomposition during alkaline treatment rather than assuming complete conversion.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sulfite oxidation and nitrile reduction have a valid net stoichiometry. However, naming sulfite-ferrocyanide photochemistry does not establish selective lactaldehyde production from this substrate. The downstream Strecker and acidic hydrolysis sequence is chemically credible, subject to concentration, pH, and temperature requirements that are not supplied.
suggestions: Specify ferrocyanide availability, concentration, irradiation spectrum, and redox turnover, and measure lactaldehyde selectivity.
Determine whether residual photoredox reagents interfere with aldehyde availability or imine trapping.
Provide a staged acidic hydrolysis protocol with measured conversion and threonine-family product recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The proposed connectivity reaches the correct amino-acid skeleton without conservation violations. Its main uncertainty is selective sulfite-ferrocyanide reduction of lactonitrile. Alkaline amide hydrolysis is a sound reaction class, but sufficient alkalinity, heating, and product stability have not been established for the stated environment.
suggestions: Validate lactaldehyde production under a defined, environmentally supported sulfite-ferrocyanide irradiation regime.
Specify the pH and temperature changes needed between photochemistry, Strecker capture, and alkaline hydrolysis.
Measure hydrolysis kinetics and amino-acid survival in the actual reaction mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanohydrin storage is chemically plausible. rxn_007 is best interpreted as reversible aldehyde release followed by imination, rather than a demonstrated elementary displacement. Productive release and imine trapping require kinetic and equilibrium support. This branch retains the photoreduction bottleneck and does not independently validate a different amino-acid-forming mechanism.
suggestions: Establish selective lactonitrile photoreduction before relying on downstream reservoir behavior.
Measure cyanohydrin storage, release, and aminonitrile capture rates as functions of ammonia, cyanide, pH, and concentration.
Demonstrate that acidic hydrolysis produces recoverable threonine-family amino acids from the resulting mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The reservoir-to-Strecker sequence is balanced and mechanistically plausible as coupled equilibria. Its operational benefit is unproven because cyanohydrin retention must be compatible with sufficient aldehyde release and imine trapping. Selective photoreduction and adequately rapid alkaline hydrolysis remain unresolved requirements.
suggestions: Measure lactaldehyde production and survival under the proposed sulfide photochemistry.
Show net transfer from the cyanohydrin pool into aminonitrile under specified ammonia and cyanide activities.
Identify a realistic alkaline heating regime and quantify conversion, decomposition, and amino-acid recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The pathway correctly returns the cyanohydrin reservoir to the shared imine manifold. Conservation is satisfied, but neither substrate-specific photoreduction nor productive reservoir release is established here. Residual sulfite chemistry and the change to acidic hydrolysis require operational characterization, not an assumption that all surface conditions are interchangeable.
suggestions: Validate lactonitrile reduction with specified ferrocyanide availability and irradiation conditions.
Quantify free lactaldehyde, cyanohydrin, and any sulfite-carbonyl adducts during ammonia-driven capture.
Specify the acidification and heating regime and measure threonine-family recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a valid operational variant of the same Strecker chemistry, not an independent mechanistic solution. The principal uncertainties are selective photoreduction, reservoir release into the imine manifold, and hydrolysis under a physically supported alkaline regime. The proposed product pool can include L-threonine without implying a particular stereoisomer ratio.
suggestions: Measure selective lactaldehyde formation and characterize photoredox-mixture carryover.
Demonstrate productive cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile conversion with measured equilibrium and kinetic data.
Provide alkaline hydrolysis conditions, their environmental source, and an amino-acid yield and stability assessment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydantoin capture and hydrolysis provide coherent, balanced connectivity. Bucherer-Bergs capture nevertheless requires a suitable carbonate/ammonia regime, not merely CO2 availability. Hydrothermal labeling does not establish sufficiently rapid ring opening or N-carbamoyl removal before degradation. This branch adds a substantial deprotection uncertainty to the shared photoreduction bottleneck.
suggestions: Validate selective sulfide-driven lactonitrile reduction and hydantoin formation under specified carbonate/ammonia conditions.
Measure nonenzymatic ring-opening and decarbamoylation rates across environmentally justified pH, temperature, and residence-time ranges.
Specify a physical surface-to-hydrothermal transfer mechanism, dilution, pressure, and a temperature window allowing amino-acid survival.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydantoin route has no conservation defect and is plausible at the reaction-class level. Selective sulfite-ferrocyanide photoreduction remains unverified for lactonitrile, while hydantoin deprotection requires substrate-specific kinetic evidence. No physical transfer or hydrothermal operating window is supplied to establish recoverable threonine production.
suggestions: Specify ferrocyanide supply and photochemical turnover and measure lactaldehyde selectivity.
Demonstrate hydantoin capture and subsequent nonenzymatic deprotection in representative mixtures, including residual photoredox reagents.
Define transfer, dilution, fluid composition, temperature, pressure, and residence time, and compare deprotection rates with product degradation.

evaluation.network_feedback: Network validity is high: the 21 molecule nodes and 13 reaction nodes form a connected graph with consistent IDs and coherent carbon-skeleton construction. The deterministic check establishes conservation for every reaction; the inferred coefficients are reasonable, including those required by S8 and aggregate stereoisomer bookkeeping. They do not establish stereoisomer proportions. The complete network remains conditional because every target-producing route depends on selective lactonitrile-to-lactaldehyde photoreduction, and the hydantoin branches additionally depend on sufficiently rapid nonenzymatic deprotection. Surface and Hydrothermal labels are too broad to verify irradiation, reagent and catalyst availability, pH, temperature, volatile retention, or transfer compatibility. The acknowledged limitations are appropriate, but acknowledgment does not substitute for experimental validation. No research findings or reaction-level citations were supplied, so literature alignment remains unassessed. Mixed stereochemistry is not treated as failure to produce L-threonine; uncertainty concerns demonstrated formation and recoverable yield, not absence of enrichment. Problematic reaction IDs mark unresolved chemical or operational requirements, not conservation violations. Confidence is bottleneck-weighted, and the ten operational paths are not counted as independent validation. P1 is tied with P2-P4; the supplied evidence does not justify preferring either donor system or hydrolysis regime. The network is not approved because overall confidence is below 0.9.
